query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an adaptive nanolaminate surface treatment to CoCrFeNi alloy will produce a dynamic, in situ‐formed lubricious oxide glaze at high temperatures (≥600 °C) while retaining a hard, low-friction surface at room temperature, thereby reducing friction coefficient and wear rate across the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Unmodified, bulk CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix with a conventional coarse or fine grain structure as produced without surface modification.
generation.intervention: An engineered, adaptive nanolaminate surface coating applied via controlled deposition methods that is designed to gradually transform under sliding-induced heating; the laminate is structured in layers so that at ambient conditions it provides a hard, wear-resistant interface and, at elevated temperatures, reacts with ambient oxygen to form a robust, lubricious oxide glaze.
generation.conditions: Sliding contact tests under controlled loads (both low and high normal loads), a sliding speed range that produces representative frictional heating, and environmental conditions including ambient air (with oxygen) over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The multilayer (nanolaminate) architecture mediates the evolution of the near-surface microstructure by preserving a mechanically stable, dense layer at lower temperatures and facilitating the formation of a continuous and adherent oxide layer at higher temperatures.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding contact, the surface tensile and frictional stresses induce localized heating. At room temperature, the nanolaminate maintains high hardness and low shear strength. As temperature rises, controlled oxidation of the upper laminate layers leads to an in situ formation of a lubricious oxide glaze that reduces adhesion and interface shear. This self-adaptive transition switches the dominant wear mechanism from plastic deformation/adhesive wear to oxidative lubrication, aligning the friction and wear performance over the wide temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated CoCrFeNi matrix, the treated sample will exhibit a consistently lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rate across all temperatures. Specifically, at high temperatures, the formation of the oxide glaze will maintain low friction and mitigate wear despite thermal softening of the base alloy.
generation.baseline: The standard CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy without surface modification, which experiences increased friction and wear variability over the temperature range, especially at elevated temperatures due to unstable oxide layer formation and microstructural softening.
generation.boundary: Temperature: Room temperature (≈25 °C) to 800 °C; Load: Both low and high normal load conditions as used in sliding experiments; Environment: Oxidizing ambient conditions (air with typical oxygen levels) where tribo-oxidation is active.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of the oxide glaze formation and its long-term stability under cyclic sliding and varying loads remain uncertain. Additionally, the potential for thermal expansion mismatch between the laminate and substrate may affect durability over repeated thermal cycles.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi alloy samples: one set with the adaptive nanolaminate surface treatment and one set untreated as baseline. Conduct ball-on-disk sliding experiments under identical conditions, varying temperature incrementally from room temperature to 800 °C, while controlling normal loads and sliding speeds in an ambient air environment. Use SEM/EDS to characterize the worn surfaces and confirm the presence and integrity of the in situ oxide glaze on treated samples at high temperatures.
measurements: Average friction coefficient over time at each temperature
Specific wear rate measured by volume loss per unit load and sliding distance
Surface morphology and chemical composition (to detect formation and stability of the oxide glaze)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if (a) under any significantly representative load or temperature condition the treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (lower friction coefficient and wear rate) compared to the untreated baseline, or (b) the adaptive oxide glaze does not form or proves unstable at the expected high-temperature regime.

In contrast, upon wear at high temperatures (≥600 °C), the wear behavior of the material becomes quite complex, stemming from the prevalence of surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation at the friction interface [,]. High-temperature sliding tends to soften the metallic surface that endows the near-surface material susceptible to chemical instability caused by counterbody materials or environmental oxygen, triggering severe delamination wear and composition segregation at the friction interface that exacerbates wear [,]. Materials become more dependent on tribochemical protection upon high-temperature wear due to deterioration in stiffness [,]. decision.trend: Early work on high-entropy alloys revealed that tailoring the near‐surface microstructure can significantly affect tribological performance. Initial research (PMC7311485 and PMC9960858) demonstrated that grain refinement and dynamic microstructural evolution (e.g., formation of ultra‐nanocrystalline layers via dynamic amorphization) can lower friction and wear in related HEA systems, albeit under limited environmental conditions. Subsequent studies (PMC8470387 and PMC12655553) introduced alloying modifications (with elements such as W or Mo) that promoted the formation of intermetallic compounds or lubricious oxide layers at elevated temperatures. Although these interventions achieved local improvements (for example, forming a lubricious MoO2 layer that lowers friction at high temperature), none have successfully maintained low friction and wear over the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under varying load and environmental stresses.
decision.unsolved: How to design a single intervention that produces a self-adaptive lubricating mechanism which protects the sliding interface and minimizes wear consistently from room temperature up to 800 °C, despite changes in load and environmental conditions.
decision.lever: Apply a controlled, adaptive nanolaminate surface treatment engineered to form an in situ, robust and lubricious oxide glaze at high temperatures while retaining a mechanically stable, hard layer at room temperature.
decision.why: Based on the trend, previous strategies have focused either on altering the bulk microstructure (via grain refinement or alloying additions) or have triggered lubrication mechanisms that activate only in narrow temperature ranges. An engineered surface coating that is designed to dynamically transform—forming a lubricious oxide layer when exposed to high temperature sliding and maintaining integrity at lower temperatures—directly addresses the challenge of achieving consistent tribological behavior across the entire temperature regime. This single intervention lever leverages surface/interface engineering to exploit gradual, stress- and temperature-induced chemical and structural transitions, aligning with prior evidence while targeting the identified gap.
